I1 Conservative modular amalgamation results
31 October 2026

What the result establishes

Two individually consistent modules can lose distinctions merely because their shared interface is identified. No extra “bad mixed law” is needed. This investigation gives an arbitrarily large family of that failure, identifies exactly which local elements collapse, and repairs it while keeping both local theories and the abstract shared theory unchanged. The repair changes where one shared interface element lands in one module: from a larger partial identity to the distinguished image projection p.

The positive result goes beyond checking algebra tables. It lifts the construction to the actual ordered graph and interface calculus, proves a complete equality criterion for presented refinement certificates, and states separate conditions for transporting cuts. It also explains why preserving equations does not automatically preserve every factorization witness.

Independent mathematical review and original-obligation coverage review record PASS for this selected original I1 package; the imported dependency copies have also been verified. Package integrity is recorded separately. This is a useful conservative subclass, not unrestricted amalgamation, acceptance of the whole completion contract, or a higher-categorical pushout theorem. Full proofs and reproducible checks accompany this checkpoint in the ZIP.

The shared structure is real

The common graph calculus P retains the whole ordered graph, actual ordered partitions, interface objects and arrows, full operation profiles, repeated input positions and empty positions. Equal component types at two positions do not make those positions interchangeable. Coefficients decorate nonempty input occurrences; they are not a replacement for the old scalar algebra, which is specialized here to its terminal case.

For a finite coefficient monoid L, write P[L] for this enriched calculus. Substitution multiplies labels in branch order, using the same parent label for all children of that occurrence. Empty occurrences receive no coefficient. The proofs cover arbitrary finite graph bounds and finite interface categories, with no bound on arity, refinement history or finite tree depth.

The main bare amalgam shares P[C], where C is a concrete five-element monoid. Thus both graph operations and nontrivial coefficients are shared. The six-vertex calculation additionally uses nonidentity interfaces 0→1→2, cross-block edges and two equal-looking two-vertex components at different positions. It tests the intended occurrence-sensitive setting rather than a disjoint-signature substitute.

There is one necessary degenerate qualification. A failed coefficient embedding can be detected by a labelled unary identity only when a nonempty colour exists: the graph bound is at least one and the interface category has an object. With graph bound zero or an empty interface category, coefficient distinctions are invisible. The pushout construction still applies; the converse faithfulness test must not be asserted there.

A genuine pushout and its exact failure boundary

The local module A_m consists of partial maps, including partial identities y_S indexed by subsets S of m ordinary coordinates. It has 2^m+4 elements. The six-element module B adds a reverse map u to the shared maps c and e, with cu=d and uc=e. Their common theory is C={0,1,e,d,c}.

For any subset J, C embeds faithfully in A_m by sending d to y_J; its other elements keep their specified images. C also embeds faithfully in B. Each input has a finite convergent multiplication-table presentation. Nevertheless, their bare pushout Q_J identifies exactly one block:

    I_J = {y_S : S is a subset of J}.

All other A_m elements remain distinct, and B remains injective. The pushout has 2^m−2^|J|+6 elements. Consequently BOTH local maps are faithful exactly when J is empty. This is an exact ideal collapse, not coordinate deletion: for J={1}, y_empty and y_{1} merge, but y_{2} and y_{1,2} need not merge.

For J containing all m coordinates, all 2^m partial identities collapse. The cause is visible in the word y_S c u. Multiplying its first two factors gives cu=y_J; multiplying its last two gives y_S y_J=y_S. Both routes use only local equations and the shared identification. Their equality forces previously distinct A_m operations to become equal. B survives, so the result does not incorrectly report collapse on both sides.

The repair keeps A_m, B and C unchanged and sends d instead to p=y_empty. The concrete pushout is then M=A_m together with u; both local maps are faithful and their intersection is exactly C. The troublesome peak now joins because y_S p=p. Changing the shared embedding is essential: one cannot retain the bad identification and simultaneously preserve distinctions it logically destroys.

The graph lifting theorem proves that P[Q_J] is the actual pushout of P[A_m] and P[B] over P[C] in the declared category of fixed-colour nonsymmetric multicategories under P. Its universal property concerns all compatible strict maps in that category, not merely a chosen semantic model. The proof converts such maps into monoid maps to families of unary operations commuting with the old graph generators. This supplies the required universal factorization without assuming conservativity in advance.

Mixed laws are a different construction

A second positive construction specifies a crossing table λ:B×A→A×B, rewriting a B label followed by an A label into A-before-B order. This is universal only among compatible maps satisfying that extra mixed law. It is not the unconstrained pushout.

The complete finite coefficient criterion checks units and the two competing reductions of BAA and BBA triples. Same-channel triples use local associativity. Word length followed by the number of out-of-order BA pairs proves termination; the listed overlaps then prove unique AB normal pairs for all words. Both local factors embed. Conversely, failure of a listed check identifies distinct proposed normal pairs, although it need not collapse a pure factor.

A genuinely noncommuting positive family uses cyclic A=C_n and B=C_2 acting by inversion, for n≥3. The comparison with relation sa=a^r s instead has cyclic image of order gcd(n,r²−1); both factors embed exactly when r²=1 modulo n. Taking r=2 and n=5^k gives unbounded collapse, while inversion repairs it. This illustrates a sharp mixed-law boundary, but does not replace the genuine bare-interface failure above. Matched-pair and semidirect-product algebra are classical foundations, not claimed discoveries.

What refinement equality actually means

Having unique operation normal forms is not yet a proof that arbitrary refinement certificates agree. The construction therefore starts with actual syntax: graph trees, primitive grafts at specified occurrences, contextual equation steps and inverses of equation steps. Its relations are independently generated, rather than defined as “whatever has the same semantic answer.”

A combined well-founded measure proves termination even when moving a coefficient through a cut duplicates its label. The critical diagrams include ordinary graph association and units, coefficient table and crossing overlaps, multiplication against distribution, and crossing against branching distribution. Disjoint and variable-overlap squares are included. Every active child receives the same crossing result, so a parent choice is never replaced by unrelated child choices.

Two further relation families connect equations with grafting: MOut moves an equation past a graft at the outer frontier; MIn compares inserting the two sides of a bare equation at an actual source occurrence. Induction extends these finite schemas to arbitrary finite forests and substituted contexts. Removing MIn leaves distinct paths with identical semantic refinements; a graft-count invariant proves this. Removing only mixed-sorting MIn also fails, as a separate coefficient-weight invariant shows. Ordinary confluence alone cannot supply these missing relations.

The resulting equality test is precise: normalize EACH forest entry at its ORIGINAL source slot and compare the entire ordered family. Retain each entry's own frontier, actual partition, grades, interfaces and active coefficient labels. Equality of the final operation or root product is insufficient. For example, deleting the first of two empty slots versus deleting the second can have the same endpoint but different entry tuples. An absorbing coefficient likewise permits distinct entry labels with the same root product.

The raw-object completion is equivalent to the independently defined refinement category Ref; restricting to normal objects gives an isomorphism. It is not literal equality of directed rewrite strings. Injective coefficient maps give faithful local certificate transfer. A global certificate has a specified local representative precisely when its endpoints and complete normal entries lie in that local image.

For the bare Q_J family, this theorem uses the explicitly chosen FULL multiplication-table presentation of Q_J, with its own generated critical diagrams and MOut/MIn completion. Local presentations map into that completion. The operation pushout does not imply that the uncompleted raw union of local equation paths is already coherent, nor establish a two-dimensional pushout universal property.

Cuts require more information

A flattened refinement arrow retains its original-slot operation tuple, not every intermediate step of execution. A marked cut record retains the whole marked tree and every factor. Normalize within each marked factor, never across a marked boundary. Foreign inverse factors can disappear from a flattened tuple while remaining genuinely foreign factors of a marked cut. These are different fullness questions.

For semidirect coefficients A⋊B with B acting by automorphisms, there is an exact source-fixed cut bijection on every actual finite old tree. Transport each A edge label by the accumulated B action strictly above that edge; retain the entire B edge array. The transformed A and B arrays satisfy separate branch-product equations. The inverse uses the retained B prefixes to undo the action and recover every original factor, including intermediate factors.

This is a B-dependent coordinate bijection, not a multiplicative projection to A. It respects insertion and contraction through the action identities, with one shared parent for all descendants. In the six-vertex inversion example, outer label (1,1) and inner label (2,0) produce (4,1) modulo five, not the naive first-coordinate sum three.

An injective local embedding reflects exactly those marked records whose EVERY factor belongs to the local image. It need not capture all ambient cuts of a local source. A local unit can factor through foreign group elements and their inverses; in the repaired bare pushout, local p has the ambient cut cu=p with u outside A_m. Full marked-cut fibres require the additional factor-closure condition: if xy is local, both x and y must be local. In the selected non-erasing geometry this condition is sufficient for all finite trees and necessary for unrestricted binary unary cuts.

Interface preservation is not interface lifting

A proposed interface map must preserve multiplication and the crossing law, or equivalently the relevant group action in the semidirect case. It must separately satisfy the actual old graph, profile, occurrence and restriction squares. Neither set of checks replaces the other.

Preservation gives forward transport. Lifting a prescribed target cut at a fixed source requires more: the allowed parent lifts for ALL children must have a common intersection. Separate successful lifts for each child are insufficient because the parent is shared. Finite coefficient tables give a finite, possibly exponential, check of these simultaneous constraints; recursive application gives all-tree lifting. Old geometry needs its own fixed-source lifting property.

Surjective group homomorphisms provide a useful noninvertible positive case: every allowed parent fibre works simultaneously. Conversely, all-root group cut lifting forces surjectivity. Such lifts need not be unique.

Coordinate restriction in the repaired partial-map family gives the contrasting sharp failure. Deleting coordinate k sends y_{k} to p and preserves every equation. But the target cut cu=p cannot lift at source y_{k}: the only candidate factors are c and u, whose product is p, not y_{k}. Unrestricted all-root lifting holds exactly when no coordinate is deleted. Coordinate permutations, by contrast, give genuine invertible transport.

Evidence and claim boundary

The independent finite suite reports PASS for 63 partial-map interfaces, 126 cyclic parameter cases, 5,236 length-three word peaks, 185 typed graph peak pairs, 573 tested occurrence squares, 8,576 accumulated-action tree arrays and 26 coordinate-restriction failures. These are named finite regressions, not an exhaustive enumeration of proof-path quotients. Separate replay and source pins make their provenance checkable. The universal properties and arbitrary-parameter, all-depth claims rest on the analytic proofs and independent mathematical review, not those counts alone.

The baseline comparison credits matched products, coherent rewriting and structured/decorated cospans under their actual hypotheses. Those frameworks do not automatically supply this full-profile conservative graph pushout, original-slot certificate criterion or correlated cut-lifting boundary. No general novelty, new Lean formalization, hardware result, unrestricted descent theorem or closure of neighboring obligations is claimed.

The practical conclusion is a selected original-I1 result with explicit acceptance conditions, a real interface-identification obstruction, a same-local-theory repair, and usable tests separating equation conservativity, refinement coherence and cut reflection. The accompanying proof package supplies the details needed to audit those distinctions rather than asking the reader to infer them from a successful table calculation.
